chapters.summary: Even amid suffering Job holds fast to his integrity; a scene in heaven reveals that God permits Satan to test him, displaying the testing and faithfulness that mark true faith.
keyPoints: Job is a blameless man in the land of Uz who fears God and turns away from evil, blessed with seven sons, three daughters, and great wealth.
Satan challenges God, claiming that Job's piety is only because of his material blessings; God permits Satan to test Job, but forbids him to touch Job's body.
In the disaster that strips him of his possessions and his children, Job still praises God and does not sin with his lips.
chapters.application: When we face loss and testing in life, let us follow Job's example: hold fast to our faith in God even in pain, trust that his purposes are good, and respond to everything with worship.

chapters.summary: Satan tests Job again, striking him with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head; yet in his suffering Job still holds fast to his integrity and does not sin with his lips.
keyPoints: God allows Satan to attack Job once more, but forbids him to take Job's life.
Job sits among the ashes scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery; when his wife urges him to curse God, he still holds fast to his faith.
Three friends come to comfort him; seeing his suffering, they weep aloud and sit with him for seven days and seven nights.
chapters.application: In the heaviest suffering, let us follow Job's example: not sin with our lips, not curse God, trust that his purposes are good, and find comfort among fellow believers.

chapters.summary: In the depths of his anguish, Job curses the day of his birth, giving voice to his despair over life and his longing for death.
keyPoints: Job opens his mouth to curse the day of his birth, wishing that day had turned to darkness.
He longs never to have been born, or to have died at birth, so as to escape his suffering.
Job's lament reveals the anguish of the human soul under extreme suffering.
chapters.application: In our pain, we may pour out our true feelings to God, but let us also remember that he is the source of comfort and hope.

chapters.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite speaks for the first time, arguing that suffering comes from sin, and urges Job to turn back to God.
keyPoints: Eliphaz gently points out that Job once taught and strengthened others, yet now grows discouraged under his own suffering.
He claims to have received a secret revelation, stressing that no one can be righteous before God.
Eliphaz regards suffering as God's discipline and urges Job to confess and repent so that he may find peace.
chapters.application: When a friend is suffering, let us weigh our words carefully, avoid quick judgment, and instead offer our presence and a listening ear, guiding them to look to God's mercy and wisdom.

chapters.summary: Eliphaz urges Job to seek God, insisting that suffering comes from sin, but that God will surely save the one who repents and will bless him.
keyPoints: Calamity befalls the fool, but God will surely save those who call upon him.
Blessed is the one whom God corrects; his discipline should not be despised.
God will heal the wounded and grant them peace and abundance.
chapters.application: When facing suffering, humbly call upon God, trusting that his discipline flows from love, and wait for his deliverance and blessing.

chapters.summary: In his pain Job pours out his heart, voicing his despair and his disappointment with his friends' comfort, yet he has not given up appealing to God.
keyPoints: Job feels his suffering so keenly that his words come out rash, for the arrows of God have pierced him.
He complains that his friends are like a stream that runs dry, unable to give him real comfort.
Job insists on his innocence and longs for God to end his life.
chapters.application: In our pain we may be honest with God, but let us also be understanding of our friends' limitations, and remain confident that God still hears our cries.

chapters.summary: In his deep anguish Job pours out his heart to God, lamenting that life is short and full of hardship, and questioning why God watches and tests humanity so closely.
keyPoints: Job compares life to a hired servant or a slave, expressing his toil and hopelessness.
He describes the pain of his rotting flesh and sleepless nights, longing for death to bring release.
Job asks God why he will not pardon his transgressions, feeling terrified and watched by him.
chapters.application: When we are in distress, we can follow Job's example and be honest with God without hiding our pain; at the same time, let us trust that God remains near us -- even when we cannot feel his presence, he has never left.

chapters.summary: Job's friend Bildad advises him from the traditional view of retribution, arguing that his suffering comes from sin, calling him to seek God, and insisting that God will not forsake the blameless.
keyPoints: Bildad points out that God is just and never perverts what is right, implying that Job's suffering must be because of sin.
He urges Job that if he is pure and upright, God will surely rise up for him and restore his righteous estate.
Appealing to the wisdom of former generations, he insists that the wicked will surely perish, but the blameless will surely be blessed.
chapters.application: When we suffer, we can easily accept others' quick judgments; instead, let us humbly seek God, trust in his grace and justice, and refrain from hastily judging ourselves or others.

chapters.summary: Job answers his friends, acknowledging God's great power, but laments that no one can be justified before God, and voices his confusion over God's justice.
keyPoints: Job acknowledges that God's power is limitless and no one can resist him.
Job laments that no one can argue his case with God -- even if he were righteous, it would do him no good.
Job questions why God allows the innocent to suffer, revealing the turmoil within his heart.
chapters.application: In suffering, though we may be confused, we can pour out our hearts freely to God, trust in his sovereignty, and hold on to faith even when we do not understand.

chapters.summary: In his pain Job pours out his heart to God, questioning why God treats him this way, while pleading with God to remember his affliction before judgment falls.
keyPoints: Job loathes his own life and pours out his complaint to God, giving voice to his inner despair.
He asks God whether it pleases him to oppress and despise him, lamenting that God's hand lies heavy upon him.
Job acknowledges God's sovereignty, yet still asks him to show mercy before judgment comes, granting him a moment's comfort.
chapters.application: In suffering, we too can follow Job's example and be honest with God without hiding our emotions, while remembering that he still reigns over all things, and waiting for his mercy.

chapters.summary: Zophar accuses Job of self-righteousness, declares that his suffering must be because of sin, and urges him to repent and turn to God -- though his words are harsh and lack compassion.
keyPoints: Zophar rebukes Job for his many useless words and his self-righteousness, unaware that God sees and examines everything.
He declares that Job's suffering must be exactly what his sin deserves, and that God has in fact punished him less than his guilt warrants.
He urges Job to put away his iniquity and set his heart on seeking God, promising peace and light, yet closes with a tone of threat.
chapters.application: When a friend is suffering, let us not rush to judgment but accompany them with gentleness, for God's purposes far exceed what we can fathom.

chapters.summary: Job answers his friends' accusations, stressing God's wisdom and sovereignty, pointing out that suffering and injustice are common on earth, yet God still rules over all.
keyPoints: Job mocks his friends' limited wisdom, saying that their words are no better than common proverbs.
Job points to the reality that the wicked prosper while the righteous suffer, challenging the traditional view of retribution.
Job declares God's wisdom and power, affirming that all things are under his control.
chapters.application: When facing suffering, let us humbly acknowledge our limitations, trust in God's sovereignty, and hold on to faith even amid confusion.

chapters.summary: In his suffering Job continues to defend himself, rebukes his friends for their false comfort, and resolves to trust God -- even if God should slay him, he will still rely on him.
keyPoints: Job rebukes his friends for comforting him with lies, calling them worthless physicians.
Job resolves to plead his case before God -- even if God should slay him, he will still trust him.
Job asks God to show him his transgressions, and is willing to lay his ways before God.
chapters.application: In hardship, let us follow Job's example, holding fast to our faith in God, laying our hearts openly before him, and trusting in his justice and love.

chapters.summary: In his suffering Job laments the shortness of human life, pleads with God for mercy, and ponders whether there is hope of resurrection after death.
keyPoints: Human life is short and full of trouble, wearisome like a hired hand's labor and fleeting like a flower that fades.
Job asks God why he will not let him live out his brief life in peace, and pleads with him to look away.
Job hopes that death might bring him rest, and wonders whether a person can live again after dying.
chapters.application: When we face the brevity and suffering of life, we can pour out our hearts honestly to God, while holding on to the hope of resurrection and trusting in his mercy through our limited days.

chapters.summary: Eliphaz rebukes Job a second time, arguing that his words reveal his guilt, insisting that calamity surely befalls the wicked, and urging him to repent.
keyPoints: Eliphaz accuses Job of speaking empty words that reveal an irreverent heart.
Eliphaz insists that God puts no trust even in his angels, much less in one so corrupt as man.
Eliphaz describes the terror and torment that fill the wicked man's life, implying that Job's suffering must be because of sin.
chapters.application: When friends misunderstand us, let us remember that God is the final judge. Do not let others' judgments shake our faith; instead, examine ourselves and hold fast to integrity.

chapters.summary: In his pain Job answers his friends, accusing them of lacking compassion, while pouring out his innocence and grief before God.
keyPoints: Job calls his friends 'miserable comforters,' feeling that they only add to his suffering.
He describes God attacking him as an enemy would, yet he still insists on his own innocence.
Job longs for a witness in heaven on his behalf, crying out to God.
themes: Pouring Out the Heart in Pain
chapters.application: When others are suffering, let us accompany them with empathy rather than rushing to accuse; even in despair, we can pour out our hearts to God, confident that he knows the wrong we have suffered.

chapters.summary: In his anguish Job laments that his life is drawing to a close, yet he still holds fast to his integrity, cries out for God to bear witness for him, and points out his friends' harshness and folly.
keyPoints: Job pours out his broken spirit, his life passing away like a breath, with darkness drawing near.
He rebukes his friends as mockers, yet still looks to God to plead his case.
Job declares that the upright will hold fast to their way, and those with clean hands will grow stronger and stronger.
chapters.application: Even in despair, keep pouring out your heart to God, trusting in his watchful care and justice, holding on to inner integrity, and waiting for him to act.

chapters.summary: Bildad speaks again, sharply rebuking Job and describing the tragic end of the wicked, insisting that the wicked will surely be punished by God.
keyPoints: Bildad rebukes Job for considering himself wise while regarding his friends as fools.
The light of the wicked will be put out; his flame will no longer shine, and he will fall into darkness and be caught in a snare.
The wicked will be seized by terror and consumed; his memory will vanish from the earth, and no one will mourn him.
chapters.application: When we suffer, let us not be quick to judge others; instead, let us examine ourselves, trust that God will judge justly, and hold on to faith through hardship.

chapters.summary: In his pain Job answers his friends, declaring his confidence that his Redeemer lives, and affirming that he will one day see God with his own eyes.
keyPoints: Job laments that his friends' repeated rebukes have broken his heart, and pleads with them to show him mercy.
He declares his confidence that his Redeemer lives and will stand at last upon the earth.
He warns his friends to fear God's judgment, for God will surely repay their injustice.
chapters.application: In the depths of suffering, hold fast to faith, trust that God will vindicate you, and wait for the day when you will see the Lord with your own eyes.

chapters.summary: Job's friend Zophar speaks again, insisting that though the wicked may prosper for a time, they will surely perish in the end, implying that Job's suffering is the result of sin.
keyPoints: Zophar responds impatiently to Job, reasserting that the wicked will surely be repaid.
Though the wicked may rise for a moment, they will in the end be swept away like refuse.
The wicked man's wealth and joy are short-lived, for God's judgment will surely come upon him.
chapters.application: Do not be troubled by the wicked's temporary prosperity; instead hold firmly to God's justice, keep your own integrity, and wait for him to act.

chapters.summary: Job answers his friends' accusations, pointing out that the wicked often enjoy peace in this life, challenging the traditional view of retribution, and emphasizing God's sovereignty and mystery.
keyPoints: Job asks his friends to listen closely, pointing out that their comfort has been empty and useless.
The wicked, though they despise God, prosper -- their homes are at peace and their households full of children.
Job declares that the wicked will surely be repaid in the end, though that reckoning may not be made plain in this life.
chapters.application: When we encounter injustice or see the wicked prosper, let us not rush to judgment, but humbly trust in God's sovereignty, hold on to faith amid suffering, and wait for his purposes to be fulfilled.

chapters.summary: Eliphaz the Temanite accuses Job of suffering because of sin, and urges him to know God and turn back to him in repentance, so that he may be restored and blessed.
keyPoints: Eliphaz believes Job's suffering stems from sin and calls on him to repent.
He stresses God's justice and transcendence, insisting that no human deed can add anything to God.
He exhorts Job to return to the Almighty and humbly accept correction, promising that he will then find peace and blessing.
chapters.application: When we face hardship, let us not be quick to blame others or ourselves; instead, let us examine our hearts, humbly seek God, and trust that he will guide us back to the right path and grant us peace and blessing.

chapters.summary: In his pain Job longs to come before God and plead his case, confident that God knows his ways, and that he will come forth purer for having been tested.
keyPoints: Job complains that he cannot find God, yet longs to lay his case before him.
Job is confident that God knows his conduct, and that when he has been tried, he will come forth as gold.
Even in darkness Job holds fast to God's commands and treasures his words.
chapters.application: When God seems to be hiding himself, still hold fast to faith, trusting that his testing has a good purpose and will refine us to greater purity.

chapters.summary: Job questions why God does not judge the wicked, describes the many crimes of those who run rampant and oppress the poor, and points out that their end will still be destruction.
keyPoints: Job is puzzled that God does not judge the wicked according to justice, while they go on enjoying peace.
He paints a vivid picture of the wicked robbing orphans and oppressing the poor.
Though the wicked flourish for a time, they will in the end be blown away like chaff before the wind.
chapters.application: When the wicked seem to prevail, we may easily doubt God's justice; but God has his appointed time, and he will surely judge. Let us hold fast to faith and not be shaken by circumstances.

chapters.summary: Bildad answers briefly, stressing God's supreme majesty and humanity's lowliness and unrighteousness -- no one can be justified before God.
keyPoints: Bildad points out that dominion and awe belong to God; his majesty is beyond measure.
Even the moon and stars are not pure in God's sight -- how much less man, who is but a maggot, a worm.
He insists that no one can be righteous before God; all we can do is bow down in awe.
chapters.application: Let us humbly acknowledge our own limitations and impurity, refrain from boasting in our own strength, and look solely to God's mercy and salvation.

chapters.summary: Job answers Bildad, emphasizing that God's sovereignty and mystery far exceed human understanding.
keyPoints: Job mocks his friend's useless help, showing that he himself well knows God's great power.
He describes God's wondrous works in the universe, such as hanging the earth on nothing and ruling over the realm of the dead.
He acknowledges that God's works cannot be fathomed, and all we can do is stand in awe.
chapters.application: When facing suffering we cannot understand, let us humbly trust in God, for his wisdom far exceeds ours, and his works will in the end be made plain.

chapters.summary: In his suffering Job holds fast to his integrity, declaring that the wicked will surely be repaid, while resolving never to abandon his reverence for God.
keyPoints: Job charges his friends with making God out to be unjust, while insisting that he himself will hold to his integrity until death.
He acknowledges that though the wicked may prosper for a time, God will surely cut them off in the end.
Job declares that his hands are free of wrongdoing and his heart does not reproach him.
chapters.application: In suffering, let us follow Job's example: never abandon integrity because of circumstances, trust that God will judge justly, and face each day with a clean heart.

chapters.summary: This chapter is a poem on wisdom, declaring that wisdom surpasses all gold, silver, and precious stones, and that the fear of the Lord alone is the beginning of wisdom.
keyPoints: Humanity can mine gold and silver from the earth, yet cannot find the worth of wisdom there.
Wisdom cannot be bought with gold, nor can it be found in the land of the living.
God alone knows the way to wisdom; to fear the Lord is wisdom, and to turn from evil is understanding.
chapters.application: In our pursuit of knowledge and wealth, let us build on the foundation of reverence for God, turn away from evil, and obtain true wisdom and peace.

chapters.summary: Job recalls the good days of the past when he enjoyed God's favor and the respect of others, and laments his present suffering and loss.
keyPoints: Job longs to return to the days when he walked closely with God.
He recalls how he was once honored by everyone because of his righteousness and integrity.
Job contrasts his once-blessed condition with his present pain, giving voice to the grief within his heart.
chapters.application: When we face hardship, we can follow Job's example and be honest with God, while trusting that his grace is sufficient and that he remains with us even in suffering.

chapters.summary: In his suffering Job laments that he has gone from being honored to being mocked by everyone, pouring out the pain and despair within his heart.
keyPoints: Job laments that he is now mocked by men younger than himself, men who were once held in contempt.
He describes their poverty and lowliness -- driven out and wandering, scraping out a living in desolate places.
Job feels deep anguish, for he once helped the afflicted, and now finds himself attacked by them instead.
chapters.application: When we face hardship and humiliation, we can follow Job's example and pour out our hearts to God; he is our refuge and will walk with us through our distress.

chapters.summary: In his suffering Job pleads his innocence, listing the ways he has turned away from sin and held fast to integrity and reverence for God.
keyPoints: Job made a covenant with his eyes, to keep himself from lustful thoughts and wrongdoing.
He dealt honestly with others, never oppressing his servants, and showed mercy to the poor.
He maintains that he never trusted in his wealth, nor secretly worshiped idols.
chapters.application: When we are in hardship, we can follow Job's example, examining our own conduct, holding fast to integrity, and trusting that God sees everything.

chapters.summary: Elihu grows angry that Job's three friends have found no answer for him, and begins to insert his own views into the conversation.
keyPoints: Elihu becomes angry because the three friends have nothing left to say.
Though he acknowledges he is young, he claims he has wisdom that must be spoken.
He rebukes the three friends for failing to refute Job, yet does not directly condemn Job himself.
chapters.application: When others are caught in endless argument, let us listen humbly, refrain from rushing to speak, and respond with gentle wisdom, rather than losing our composure in anger.

chapters.summary: Elihu urges Job to listen closely, pointing out that God speaks to people through dreams and through suffering, sending a messenger to lead them to repentance and salvation.
keyPoints: Elihu asks Job to listen, declaring that his own words come from an upright heart.
God warns people through dreams or visions, to keep them from pride.
When a person suffers, God sends a messenger to show him the way he should go, redeeming him from going down to the pit.
chapters.application: When life brings suffering or confusion, let us quiet our hearts to listen for God's reminders -- through Scripture, the Spirit, or others -- and turn back in time to experience his salvation and grace.

chapters.summary: Elihu continues speaking, stressing that God rules with justice, refuting Job's self-righteousness, and urging people to fear God.
keyPoints: Elihu calls on the wise to listen to him and discern the error in Job's words.
He stresses that God will surely not do wrong; the Almighty repays every person according to what they have done.
He points out that Job's complaints under suffering amount, in fact, to an improper stance of arguing with God.
chapters.application: When facing injustice or suffering, trust in God's justice, examine yourself, avoid complaining, and wait for God to act with a reverent heart.

chapters.summary: Elihu answers Job, pointing out that no one's conduct can put God under obligation, that God's greatness far exceeds human understanding, and that people should wait quietly.
keyPoints: Elihu rebukes Job for considering himself righteous, insisting that no one can argue a case with God.
He stresses God's exalted majesty -- human good or evil does not affect God, but it does affect the person themselves.
He calls on Job to look to God in his suffering, for God will not listen to an empty cry.
chapters.application: When facing injustice or suffering, do not interrogate God; instead, humbly examine yourself and wait quietly for his deliverance.

chapters.summary: Elihu continues to defend God, emphasizing his great power and justice, and exhorting Job to turn to God in his suffering.
keyPoints: Elihu points out that God is just; he never despises anyone, yet he will not let the wicked live.
God uses suffering to instruct people, turning them away from sin so they may enjoy peace.
He exhorts Job not to despise God's discipline because of his suffering, but to hold God in reverence.
chapters.application: In suffering, meditate on God's justice and love, humbly accept his correction, turn away from sin, and return to him -- he will surely grant peace and salvation.

chapters.summary: This chapter records Elihu continuing to speak of God's majesty, using thunder, lightning, wind, and snow to show that no one can fathom God's works, and that we should hold him in reverence.
keyPoints: Elihu describes the thunder and lightning, revealing God's majesty and power.
God governs the earth with wind, snow, and frost, yet no one can comprehend his workings.
He exhorts Job to fear God, for his works are wondrous and awe-inspiring.
chapters.application: When we behold the wonders of nature, let us hold a humble and reverent heart, acknowledging that God's wisdom far exceeds ours, and trust in his plan even amid hardship.

chapters.summary: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, posing a series of questions about the creation of the universe and the wonders of nature, showing that his wisdom far exceeds human understanding.
keyPoints: God questions Job with a series of rhetorical questions, exposing the limits of human knowledge.
He describes the mysteries of creation -- the foundations of the earth, the boundaries of the sea -- emphasizing his sovereignty.
Before God's majesty Job is left speechless, acknowledging his own ignorance.
chapters.application: When we are confused and cannot understand, let us remember that God governs all things, that his wisdom far exceeds ours, and learn to respond with humble trust.

chapters.summary: God questions Job further with the wild goat, the wild donkey, the wild ox, the ostrich, the horse, and the eagle, showing that his wisdom and sovereignty far exceed human understanding.
keyPoints: God questions Job using the wonders of the animal world, displaying his creative wisdom.
Wild creatures like the donkey and the ox, free and untamed, reveal the unique instincts God has given to every living thing.
The habits of the ostrich, the horse, and the eagle reveal that God's sovereignty transcends human logic.
chapters.application: When life's questions are hard to answer, remember God's mighty power in creating all things, humbly trust in his guidance, and find rest in the unknown.

chapters.summary: The LORD continues to answer Job, using his power and his works of creation to show that no one can argue a case with God, and challenging Job to face his majesty.
keyPoints: God asks Job whether he would instruct the Almighty, and demands that whoever would argue with God must answer.
God points to Behemoth, the mighty creature he made, whose strength and power no one can tame.
Through this God leads Job to recognize his own smallness and to learn humble submission.
chapters.application: When facing suffering and confusion, acknowledge that God's wisdom far exceeds ours, and learn to trust his guidance with a humble heart rather than questioning him according to our own judgment.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes God pointing to Leviathan, the great creature, to display his mighty creative power -- no one can subdue it -- leading Job to recognize his own limitation and God's supreme sovereignty.
keyPoints: God asks Job whether he can draw out Leviathan with a fishhook, exposing human powerlessness.
Leviathan's scales, teeth, and strength have no equal, symbolizing God's power, which no one can challenge.
If a person fears even Leviathan, how much more should they stand in awe of the God who created it.
chapters.application: When facing life's difficulties, acknowledge your own limitations, trust in God's sovereignty, and find peace in reverence for him.

chapters.summary: Job answers God out of the whirlwind, acknowledging his own ignorance, and repenting because he has now seen God with his own eyes; God then restores his fortunes and blesses him.
keyPoints: Job acknowledges that God can do all things, and that no purpose of his can be thwarted.
Job repents that he once spoke words of ignorance that obscured God's counsel.
God restores Job's possessions and family, blessing him twice as much as before.
chapters.application: In suffering, let us humbly acknowledge our limitations, trust in God's sovereignty, and believe that in his own time he will restore us and bless us.
